extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants and attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how different transitional phrases (e.g., 'comprising', 'consisting of', 'consisting essentially of', 'having', 'composed of') affect the scope of patent claims and how to apply those meanings in claim construction, searching, and prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional phrases define claim scope (case-by-case)
rubrics_metrics.description: The transitional phrases 'comprising', 'consisting essentially of' and 'consisting of' define the scope of a claim with respect to what unrecited additional components or steps, if any, are excluded from the scope of the claim. The determination of what is or is not excluded by a transitional phrase must be made on a case-by-case basis in light of the facts of each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation depends on particular facts and the specification; no automatic rule applies beyond the general meanings of the common transitional phrases. Always read transitional language in light of the remainder of the claim and the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprising — open-ended / inclusive transition
rubrics_metrics.description: The transitional term 'comprising' (synonymous with 'including,' 'containing,' or 'characterized by') is inclusive or open-ended and does not exclude additional, unrecited elements or method steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'comprising' when an open-ended claim is intended. Case law examples: courts have held 'comprising' permits additional steps (Invitrogen) and additional components (Gillette: a claim 'comprising' guard, cap and group of blades encompassed razors with more than three blades). Even when a Markush group is used to list alternatives, a 'comprising' transition can allow additional components functionally similar to listed members (Amgen v. Amneal). The term signals that named elements are essential but that other elements may be added and still be within claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consisting of — closed / exclusive transition
rubrics_metrics.description: The transitional phrase 'consisting of' excludes any element, step, or ingredient not specified in the claim (except for ordinary impurities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'consisting of' to close the claim to unrecited elements. A claim depending from a claim that 'consists of' the recited elements cannot add another element or step. However, closure under 'consisting of' applies to the clause in which it appears (a body-clause 'consisting of' creates an exceptionally strong presumption that that claim term is closed to unrecited elements), and does not necessarily exclude other separate elements of the claim as a whole. There are factual exceptions (e.g., Norian v. Stryker: an added spatula unrelated to the claimed invention did not avoid infringement). For Markush group selections, 'consisting of' indicates a closed group for selection unless the claim includes qualifying language indicating combinations/mixtures are intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consisting essentially of — middle-ground transition (material-effect test)
rubrics_metrics.description: The transitional phrase 'consisting essentially of' limits the scope of a claim to the specified materials or steps 'and those that do not materially affect the basic and novel characteristic(s)' of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Consisting essentially of' occupies a middle ground between 'consisting of' (closed) and 'comprising' (open). To exclude additional steps or components under this phrase, the applicant must show that the additional matter would materially change the basic and novel characteristics of the invention. If the specification does not identify what the basic and novel characteristics are, courts may construe 'consisting essentially of' as equivalent to 'comprising' for purposes of 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103. Specification statements (e.g., numerical limits or discussion of deleterious effects) can establish what materially alters the invention (see AK Steel example). The applicant bears the burden to establish exclusion by 'consisting essentially of.' This language can be used for compositions or method steps (Ex parte Hoffman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush groups and mixtures — presumption of closed group; drafting to include mixtures
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim element defined by selection from a group of alternatives (a Markush grouping) is presumed closed to alternatives outside the list unless qualifying language indicates otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the drafter intends to encompass combinations or mixtures of the alternatives in a Markush group, include qualifying language such as 'at least one member selected from the group' or 'or mixtures thereof.' In the absence of such language, there is a presumption that the Markush group is closed to combinations or mixtures. Intrinsic evidence in dependent claims or specification statements can overcome this presumption (see Multilayer Stretch Cling Film). For open claims using 'comprising', additional functionally similar components outside the Markush group may still be within scope (see Amgen v. Amneal). See MPEP § 2117 for further discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Location of transition (preamble vs clause) matters
rubrics_metrics.description: When 'consisting of' (or other transitional language) appears in a clause of the body of a claim rather than immediately following the preamble, there is an exceptionally strong presumption that the term set off with 'consisting of' is closed to unrecited elements of that clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A body-clause 'consisting of' limits only the element set forth in that clause; it does not necessarily close the claim as a whole. Conversely, a transition immediately following the preamble (e.g., 'the apparatus consisting of:') can signal closure of the claimed combination. Always analyze the syntactic location of the transitional phrase when construing scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other transitional phrases ('having', 'composed of') — fact-specific interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitional phrases such as 'having' and 'composed of' must be interpreted in light of the specification to determine whether open or closed claim language is intended; 'composed of' may be interpreted like either 'consisting of' or 'consisting essentially of' depending on the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume a uniform meaning for less-common transitions. 'Having' has been interpreted as open in some contexts but does not create a universal presumption of openness. 'Composed of' may be treated as 'consisting of' or 'consisting essentially of' depending on specification and evidence (see AFG Industries and Bertsch). Evaluate specification language and intrinsic/extrinsic evidence to determine intended scope.
